---
title: "Git for working on the gflownet library"
---

A practical guide to the Git commands needed to work on the
[`gflownet`](https://github.com/alexhernandezgarcia/gflownet) library:
getting the code, moving between branches, checking out pull requests,
keeping personal notes, and comparing branches.

New to Git? Start with [Git basics](git-basics.qmd).

## How Git stores your work

A change goes through four places:

| Place | What it is | Moved there with |
|---|---|---|
| **Working directory** | the files in your folder, as you edit them | (just edit) |
| **Staging area** | the changes selected for the next commit | `git add` |
| **Local repository** | the commit history, on your laptop only | `git commit` |
| **Remote** (`origin`) | the repository on GitHub | `git push` |

- **Staged** changes will go into the next commit. **Unstaged** changes
  are edits that you haven't selected yet: they stay in your folder and
  are not saved in the history.
- A commit is saved on your laptop only. Nothing reaches GitHub until you
  `git push`.
- `git status` tells you, at any time, which files are modified, staged
  or untracked.

## Getting the code

```bash
# Clone with SSH (needs an SSH key set up on GitHub)
git clone git@github.com:alexhernandezgarcia/gflownet.git
cd gflownet

# Or with HTTPS, choosing the folder name (the last argument)
git clone https://github.com/alexhernandezgarcia/gflownet.git gflownet-lib
cd gflownet-lib
```

`origin` is the name Git gives to the repository you cloned from.

## Branches

```bash
# Download the latest information about the remote branches
# (does not change your files)
git fetch origin

# Switch to an existing branch, e.g. ising
git switch ising

# Bring your local ising up to date with GitHub
git pull origin ising

# Create a NEW branch from where you are, and switch to it
git switch -c ising-logz-unbiased

# List local branches (the current one is marked with *)
git branch

# Same, with the last commit of each branch and the remote branch it
# tracks, e.g. [origin/main: behind 3]
git branch -vv

# Go back to main
git switch main
```

`git switch` swaps the contents of your folder to match another branch:
Git rewrites the files so that they are exactly as they are on that
branch. `-c` stands for **create**.

::: {.callout-warning}
Commit or stash your changes before switching. Git refuses to switch if
uncommitted changes would be overwritten by the other branch.
:::

## Checking out a pull request

A pull request (PR) can be fetched into a local branch by its number,
even when it comes from someone else's fork:

```bash
# Fetch PR #446 into a new local branch called composite-tree
git fetch origin pull/446/head:composite-tree

git branch                 # check that the branch exists
git switch composite-tree  # Switched to branch 'composite-tree'
```

To get later updates of the PR, fetch it again from `main` (you can't
fetch into the branch you are on), then switch back:

```bash
git switch main
git fetch origin pull/446/head:composite-tree
git switch composite-tree
```

## Saving your work: add and commit

```bash
git status                  # what changed?
git diff                    # unstaged changes, line by line
git add gflownet/envs/scrabble.py   # stage one file
git add .                   # or stage every change in this folder
git diff --staged           # what will go into the commit
git commit -m "Improve tree environment"   # -m = commit message
```

You don't have to commit all your changes: stage only the files you
want. `git add -p` goes further and lets you pick individual parts of a
file.

## Keeping personal notes on a branch

To annotate the library code (comments, study notes) without touching
the real branches, put the notes on a branch of their own:

```bash
git switch -c my-notes
# ... add comments to gflownet/envs/scrabble.py ...
git add gflownet/envs/scrabble.py
git commit -m "My study notes on the scrabble env"
git switch main
```

Now you can go back and forth:

```bash
git switch my-notes   # scrabble.py WITH your comments
git switch main       # scrabble.py WITHOUT them (the upstream version)
```

## Putting changes aside: stash

`git stash` saves your uncommitted changes and cleans the folder, so you
can switch branches without committing half-finished work.

```bash
git stash           # put the changes aside
git switch other-branch
# ... look at something ...
git switch -        # go back to the previous branch
git stash pop       # bring the changes back
git stash list      # see what is stashed
```

## Staying up to date: rebase

When your branch (for example `my-notes`) is behind `main` on GitHub,
`git branch -vv` shows something like `[origin/main: behind 3]`. To put
your commits on top of the latest `main`:

```bash
git fetch origin
git switch my-notes
git rebase origin/main
```

Rebase replays your commits, one by one, on top of `origin/main`, so
your branch now contains everything new in `main` plus your notes.

- If a commit conflicts, Git stops. Fix the files, then
  `git add <file>` and `git rebase --continue`.
  `git rebase --abort` cancels and puts everything back as it was.
- Rebase rewrites your commits. That is fine for a local branch like
  `my-notes`, but don't rebase a branch that others have already pulled.
  `git merge origin/main` is the alternative that doesn't rewrite
  anything.

## Looking at other branches without switching

```bash
# Print a file as it is on another branch (your folder is not touched)
git show my-notes-tree:gflownet/envs/tree/tree.py | head -60

# Save that version to a file, e.g. to open it in VS Code
git show my-notes-tree:gflownet/envs/tree/tree.py > ~/Desktop/tree_notes.py

# Differences in one file between two branches (e.g. only your notes)
git diff ines/tree-categorical my-notes-tree -- gflownet/envs/tree/tree.py

# Copy a file from another branch INTO the current branch
# (careful: overwrites your version of that file)
git checkout my-notes-tree -- gflownet/envs/tree/tree.py
```

In `git show <branch>:<path>`, `<branch>` can be any branch or commit,
and `<path>` is relative to the root of the repository. `| head -60`
only keeps the first 60 lines.

## Comparing branches

`A..B` (two dots) means "the commits in `B` that are not in `A`":

```bash
# Commits of #459's branch that are not in #446's branch
git log --oneline origin/complete_envs_tree_node..origin/composite_tree_envs_add_regression

# Only the merge commits
git log --oneline --merges origin/complete_envs_tree_node..origin/composite_tree_envs_add_regression

# Files that differ between two branches
git diff --stat origin/main origin/composite_tree_envs_add_regression
```

This is how to check which commits a PR adds on top of the PR it is
built on.

## Safety: never push to the shared repository by accident

You can disable pushing to `origin` while keeping `fetch` and `pull`:

```bash
git remote set-url --push origin DISABLED
git remote -v      # fetch: the real URL, push: DISABLED
```

Any `git push` now fails. To undo it:

```bash
git remote set-url --push origin https://github.com/alexhernandezgarcia/gflownet.git
```

## Ignoring files only on your laptop

`.git/info/exclude` works like `.gitignore`, but it is local: it isn't
committed, so nobody else sees it. Use it for personal files (scratch
scripts, notes) that you don't want Git to show or add.

```bash
echo "path/to/myfile.py" >> .git/info/exclude
```

It only affects **untracked** files. A file that is already committed
stays tracked. To stop tracking it while keeping it on disk:
`git rm --cached path/to/myfile.py`.

## VS Code indicators

In the status bar at the bottom left, next to the branch name:

- **Cloud with an arrow ↑**: the branch is not published to GitHub, it
  exists only on your laptop. Clicking it publishes it, so only do that
  if you want it online (and choose a private repository).
- **`*` after the branch name** (e.g. `main*`): there are uncommitted
  changes.

## Deleting a cloned repository

A clone is just a folder: its whole history is in the hidden `.git`
folder inside. Deleting the folder deletes the local repository (not the
one on GitHub). This is a shell command, not a Git one:

```bash
rm -rf path/to/repo
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`rm -rf` deletes permanently, without a trash bin, including commits
that were never pushed. Check the path first.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| clone into a named folder | `git clone <url> <folder>` |
| what changed? | `git status`, `git diff` |
| download remote updates | `git fetch origin` |
| switch branch | `git switch <branch>` |
| create and switch | `git switch -c <new-branch>` |
| list branches with tracking info | `git branch -vv` |
| update the current branch | `git pull origin <branch>` |
| check out PR #N | `git fetch origin pull/N/head:<name>` |
| stage / commit | `git add <file>`, `git commit -m "..."` |
| put changes aside | `git stash`, `git stash pop` |
| move your commits onto the latest main | `git rebase origin/main` |
| read a file on another branch | `git show <branch>:<path>` |
| commits in B but not in A | `git log --oneline A..B` |
| disable pushing | `git remote set-url --push origin DISABLED` |
| ignore a file locally | `echo "<path>" >> .git/info/exclude` |
